result: The study found significant group differences in adaptation time constants between dyslexic and control participants in the left superior temporal lobe, right insular cortex (whole-brain analysis), and left primary auditory cortex (ROI analysis).
evaluation: Reviewers expressed concern that the study does not show 'widespread significant shorter cortical adaptation as suggested in the title' and noted that 'regions in which significant group differences are small and include high-level multimodal cortex that is not predicted by the previous work.' They unanimously requested ROI analysis focused on planum temporale where N1 generators are located, indicating the reported significant regions were insufficient or unexpected.

result: The authors claim a broadly distributed tendency for shorter adaptation in dyslexia across all cortical regions responding to tone discrimination, suggesting this is a general characteristic of cortical dynamics in dyslexia.
evaluation: Reviewers directly challenged this interpretation, stating 'Examination of the areas in which there is a decrease in tau without correction for multiple comparisons shows a widespread swathe of differences that I find difficult to reconcile with the hypothesised deficit in the sensory trace. For example, there is shorter tau in primary somatosensory cortex and motor cortex.' They questioned whether this is consistent with the anchoring deficit model.

result: Good readers performed better than dyslexic participants in the scanner (82.5% vs. 76.3%), which the authors attribute to dyslexics' impaired learning from the short pre-scan practice.
evaluation: Reviewers raised an alternative explanation that was not discussed: 'these results are due to the added acoustic noise of scanning, since continuous fMRI sampling as opposed to sparse sampling was employed. It is well known that individuals with dyslexia tend to have trouble with noise exclusion.' They requested discussion of this confounding factor.

result: The authors link their fMRI findings to previous ERP results showing faster decay of N1-P2 components in dyslexia, citing that N1 originates from planum temporale and P2 from Heschl's gyrus, with BOLD activity correlating with N1-P2 magnitude.
evaluation: Reviewers had 'difficulty reconciling these data with the previous neurophysiological data' and specifically noted that 'A specific test of this idea would require a comparison of the time constants in the generator of the N1, conventionally regarded as in planum temporale.' They unanimously requested ROI analysis focused on this region, indicating the connection to previous work was not adequately demonstrated.

result: The block design allowed measurement of adaptation dynamics in timescales independent of the sluggishness of the hemodynamic response function.
evaluation: Reviewers were 'struck by the capacity to extract adaptation and adaptation-recovery time course information from fMRI data, but it was agreed that a clearer explanation is warranted of how this can be studied using a method that has a time lag of several seconds.' This indicates skepticism about the methodological claim.

result: The authors claim their findings of faster decay of adaptation in dyslexia are consistent with Perrachione et al. 2016's findings of reduced stimulus-specific adaptation and a group x time x condition interaction in dyslexia.
evaluation: Reviewers found 'The discussion of the time course of adaptation with regards to the Perrachione et al., 2016 at the beginning of the Discussion section is confusing' and stated 'it is unclear how they reconcile this with the stimulation procedure of the Perrachione study.' They also noted that the authors should comment on the three-way interaction reported by Perrachione et al., suggesting the correspondence was not clearly established.

result: Whole-brain significance results were corrected for multiple comparisons using Monte-Carlo cluster correction with a cluster threshold of 44 voxels at p=0.05.
evaluation: Reviewers requested 'More details are also needed regarding the Monte Carlo simulations for cluster-level multiple comparison corrections to ensure that others could replicate this approach,' indicating the methodological description was insufficient for evaluation.

result: The authors propose that impaired retention in dyslexia will affect perception and impede performance in perceptual tasks involving stimulus repetitions, with reduced advantages from familiarity and impaired long-term accumulation of stimulus statistics.
evaluation: Reviewers requested that 'Some attempt should be made to explain why the decay is faster in dyslexics by fitting the results into what is already known about dyslexics' relative insensitivity to amplitude and frequency modulations,' suggesting the proposed mechanisms were not adequately connected to existing knowledge about dyslexia.
